title: One type of supernova always peaks at about the same brightness: a cosmic tape measure

cover.alt: The arm of a spiral galaxy seen by Hubble, with a dazzling star-like point of light at lower left: the supernova SN 2018gv.
cover.credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Kornmesser, M. Zamani, A. Riess and the SH0ES team · CC BY 4.0

body: A Type Ia supernova starts with a white dwarf, the dense leftover core of a star, pulling material off a companion star. When it reaches about 1.44 times the Sun’s mass, its core gets hot enough to ignite carbon fusion, and within seconds a runaway reaction tears the star apart. These explosions consistently peak at about **5 billion times** the Sun’s brightness. So by comparing how bright one really is with how faint it looks from Earth, astronomers can work out how far away its galaxy is, and use that to measure how fast the universe is expanding.

slides.alt: A spiral galaxy arm with a dazzling point of light at lower left that dims and fades away, while a small inset graph traces its brightness dropping.
slides.caption: Hubble images of supernova SN 2018gv in the galaxy NGC 2525, February 2018 to February 2019, at half speed: it outshines the galaxy’s brightest stars, then fades away.
slides.credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Kornmesser, M. Zamani, A. Riess and the SH0ES team · CC BY 4.0 · excerpt, slowed to half speed

slides.heading: How a Type Ia supernova happens

steps.label: A white dwarf orbits close to another star
It pulls material off its companion
It reaches about 1.44 times the Sun’s mass
Runaway carbon fusion blows it apart

slides.question: At its peak, a Type Ia supernova shines how many billion times brighter than the Sun?
slides.explanation: About 5 billion times. Because that peak is so consistent, how faint one looks from Earth reveals how far away it is.

slides.label: light-years to NGC 2525, the galaxy in the clip
slides.text: The supernova was first spotted in mid-January 2018. The explosion threw out matter at up to 6% of the speed of light.

slides.question: Which pulsing stars do astronomers combine with these supernovae to measure cosmic distances?
slides.explanation: Cepheids swell and shrink with a period tied to their true brightness, so they too act as standard candles on the cosmic distance ladder.
